en: A Separate Record of the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Chongfu Temple.

Explanation of the Title: the meaning of "reverence" in the verse; the meaning of "Jewel" (*ratna*) within the Buddha-Jewel; the meaning of "Treasury" (*kośa*) within the Dharma-Jewel; and its application.
"Great" has the meaning of being exclusively wholesome;
"awakening" has the meaning of both awakening and non-awakening;
and this explains the two characteristics that follow defilement.
The meaning of original enlightenment; the meaning of that which is originally present versus that which is produced through cultivation;
the seven categories of meaning within the conditions of arising and ceasing;
and one category of meaning within arising and ceasing.
The four topical divisions within the permeation of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) and the seven topical divisions within the permeation of pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*).
A brief topical outline of the text.
The fourfold meaning of the arousal of the mind within the analysis of "entering the path";
the analytical explanation of the meaning of "correct practice";
and the single meaning of the non-duality of form and mind.
The *ālayavijñāna* is explained as having the sense of being associated with afflictions;
the *tathāgatagarbha* is explained as having the sense of possessing merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and the *ālaya* is explained as the synthesis of the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
The meaning of the nine aspects;
the two meanings of *tathatā*;
and the meaning of the inconceivable aspect of the purity of wisdom.
Within the essential nature and characteristics of awakening, there is the principle of the four mirrors;
regarding the text on the mutual dependence of the beginning and the fundamental,
within the perfuming of defiled dharmas, ignorance and the deluded mind each possess two meanings.
The dependent origination of the pure portion contains four propositions:
the meaning of the dependent origination of the true and the false within the gate of arising and ceasing,
and the meaning of the Dharma-body.
The fourfold meaning of the mind and objects regarding truth and falsehood;
the meaning of the non-obstruction of the two truths;
and the meaning of the two truths.
The meaning of defilement and purity;
the Tathāgatagarbha; and the meaning of the four types of denial.
First, regarding the explanation of the title:
because the Mahāyāna possesses seven meanings, it is called the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna). It is the "One Path" because it is supreme.
The treatise states:
It is called the Mahāyāna because it is superior to the two vehicles.
Second, because it can reach the supreme state.
The treatise says:
"The Buddhas are the greatest."
This Mahāyāna is able to reach [the goal];
therefore it is called "Great.
Because it is the vehicle ridden by the three types of great beings, the treatise says:
Because all Buddhas, the Great Beings, mount this vehicle;
and because it is capable of accomplishing great matters.
The Treatise says:
Because it can extinguish the great suffering of sentient beings and bestow matters of great benefit,
it is called "Great."
It is the vehicle ridden by the five great beings,
and is also called the vehicle for many people.
The treatise says:
It is called "Great" because it is that which is mounted by Avalokiteśvara and all other great bodhisattvas;
and sixth, because it exhausts the very source and depths of all phenomena.
The Treatise says:
Because it can exhaust the very depths of all phenomena,
it is called "Great."
Because the seven methods of inclusion are complete.
The treatise states:
"As the Buddha taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is immeasurable and boundless."
For these reasons, it is called "Great.
Furthermore, another explanation states that the Mahāyāna has three meanings.
First, regarding the analysis of its name, there are four points.
First, regarding the Dharma, there are three aspects:
namely, the three greatnesses and the two vehicles,
as explained in the treatise below.
Second, there are seven [types] categorized by practice,
as explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises.
Third, there are seven categorized by persons and dharmas.
As stated in the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*,
the four direct arguments for the Great [Vehicle] take the Dharma itself as their reason.
Its meaning consists in its comprehensive inclusion;
furthermore, it distinguishes the meaning of the vehicles (yāna) and is named by means of metaphorical illustration.
Its function is to transport;
its essence is capable of lifting up in unison.
Therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"Because it rides upon the great nature,
it is called the Mahāyāna."
The commentary states:
This refers to the true nature (dharmatā) which pervades everywhere;
therefore, it is called "Great."
This refers to that which is mounted upon.
Because wondrous wisdom mounts it,
it is called a "vehicle" (yāna).
This refers to the "one who can ride" (the practitioner). It is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
As the treatise states:
It is both a vehicle and great;
thus it is called the Mahāyāna (Great Vehicle).
This refers to the capacity of the essence itself to transport [beings].
Therefore, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
Because its nature is vast and extensive, it is called "great" (*mahā*);
this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Second, regarding the essential nature, there are two aspects. First,
non-conceptual wisdom is primarily taken as the essence of the vehicle,
while it also inclusively encompasses the *tathatā* (suchness) upon which it relies, as well as other superior practices.
Secondly, it is precisely with True Suchness (tathatā) as the essence of the vehicle;
wisdom and the other factors are also subsumed therein, because they are all produced by True Suchness.
The functions of the three karmas are twofold.
First, in terms of the meaning of the three Buddha-natures,
as explained in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is that which is mounted;
the extraction [of the qualities] is the vehicle;
and the attainment of the fruit is the destination reached by the vehicle.

In this context, "vehicle" (yāna) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*) when referring to that which is mounted; it is pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*) when referring to that which enables one to mount it. Second, regarding the meaning of the cause bringing about the fruit through transport, there are three aspects:
first, its operation causes [the qualities] to increase.
The second stage transports afflictions toward extinction;
the third stage transports principle toward manifestation.
The former is the capacity.
The latter two are the objects;
these are the three virtues within nirvāṇa, namely: prajñā, vimukti, and [vimuktijñānadarśana].
The Dharma-body.
The text [explains] that this is the threefold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
First is the transformation of the single mind,
which means that true nature manifests.
Second is the transformation of the path.
This refers to the gradual increase of practice.
Third, regarding the counteractive transformation, it refers to the cessation of the obstacles of affliction.
This is the text within this treatise.
The destruction of the synthetic consciousness and so forth is transformation through cessation;
the manifestation of the dharmakāya is transformation through revelation;
and the purity of wisdom is transformation through increase.
The remaining meanings may be inferred accordingly.
First, regarding the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, there are two gates and four meanings.
Within the gate of the initial stage, that of the object and the subject:
The Mahāyāna is that which gives rise [to faith],
and faith is that which is given rise to;
therefore, it is called "the Mahāyāna’s giving rise to faith."
The second, "arousing faith," refers to that which is capable of believing;
"Mahāyāna" refers to that which is believed.
Therefore, it is called "arousing faith in the Mahāyāna."
Within the section on the two aspects of essence and function,
the first is the discernment based on subsuming function back into essence;
this refers to this very mind of faith.
This is accomplished through the internal permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and external conditions;
for it is not different from the original source,
and because it is true.
The arising of faith is itself the Mahāyāna;
therefore, it is called "Awakening Faith in the Mahāyāna.
Second, the title is explained directly in terms of its functional application.
This means that this mind of faith is vast and extensive;
therefore, it is called "great.
It proceeds from the subtle to the manifest.
Because it has the sense of "setting in motion," it is called a vehicle (*yāna*);
that is to say, it is the arousal of faith.
It is also the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is called the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda* (Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna).
Within the second verse, regarding the third point on the expression of respect:
A single verse consists of four lines. There are four ways of increasing the number [of verses]:
first, they may be combined as one whole.
This refers to the object for whom [the action] is performed.
Second, it may be divided into two:
namely, the person for whom [the action] is performed as mentioned in the preceding phrase.
The benefits accomplished by the remaining phrases are threefold,
or alternatively, divided into three: namely,
the persons for whom [the teaching] is intended, as indicated by the first phrase.
The middle two phrases constitute the practices to be cultivated;
the final phrase constitutes the virtue to be attained.
Alternatively, these four may be expanded into four [separate points].
That is to say: the first phrase refers to the person for whom [the teaching] is intended;
the second phrase refers to the faults to be abandoned;
and the third phrase refers to the accomplishment of virtue.
The virtue reached by the fourth phrase is included within the third Jewel, the Buddha Jewel;
alternatively, they may be taken together as one.
This refers to the Buddha.
Alternatively, they may be grouped into two categories:
namely, the first verse clarifies the function.
The latter two lines of the verse clarify the essence and characteristics;
alternatively, they may be taken as three,
meaning that the first two lines of the initial verse clarify the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The final phrase clarifies the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
Alternatively, there are four [bodies],
namely, within the saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment body).
The first phrase clarifies the mind;
the second phrase clarifies form.
Regarding the "treasury of internal merits" within the fourth Jewel of the Dharma:
The term "garbha" (matrix/storehouse) has three meanings.
First, it carries the sense of accumulation;
for it accumulates phenomena within and expands them.
Second is the sense of inclusion,
because it encompasses both the internal and the external.
Third is the sense of production.
Because flowing virtue accomplishes benefit,
these three meanings exist within the principle-dharma (*dharmatā*).
In relation to its own intrinsic virtue (*svabhāva-guṇa*), it possesses the first meaning.
Regarding that teaching, practice, and fruit, there are the latter two meanings;
furthermore, within practice and fruit, there are again two meanings.
Within both practice and fruit, there is the first meaning, which consists of the respective accumulation of merit.
Furthermore, there is a second sense in which the self-nature and the principle are viewed as sources;
in that the fruit is viewed as the source of practice and teaching,
and both practice and teaching are viewed as sources of the fruit.
It should be understood that the teaching, when established in relation to what precedes it, possesses the three meanings of the three attainments (*prāpti*).
Within the fifth section, the "Establishment of the Meaning" (*siddhārtha-vibhāga*),
the question is asked:

For what reason was it previously explained that within the "Greatness of Essence," this applies universally to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) without distinguishing between the defiled and the pure, nor their characteristics and functions?
It is exclusively wholesome;
it does not extend to the unwholesome. Answer:
The essence of the Great Principle is said to pervade all phenomena;
it cannot be differentiated.
If there were a separate ignorance outside of True Suchness that constituted the essence of unwholesomeness, [it would contradict this].
There are many faults;
let us illustrate them by means of two points.
First, it is identical to the non-Buddhists' adherence to the eternal nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
Because they exist inherently and do not arise from causes;
secondly, because sentient beings ultimately lack the possibility of attaining liberation.
Because that which possesses an intrinsic nature cannot be severed,
it would either arise eternally or never arise at all.
Because of this fault,
one cannot establish ignorance as having an unwholesome essence apart from True Suchness (tathatā).
Unwholesome dharmas and the like cannot also function as the characteristic or activity of *tathatā*. If they were such a characteristic or activity,
[it would follow that they are not unwholesome].
There are also many faults;
let us explain them by means of two points.
First is the fault of the confusion between cause and effect.
First, one would have to experience the fruit of suffering as a result of those wholesome causes.
Second, a noble one who has realized suchness would have to give rise to unwholesome and evil karma.
Because of this fault,
the unwholesome cannot function as the characteristic or activity of *tathatā*.
Question:
If that is so, then the unwholesome should not take suchness as its essence.
Answer: It is precisely by means of unwholesome dharmas [that it does].
Because it takes that suchness as its essence,
that which contradicts it and is dissociated from it is termed unwholesome.
Furthermore, because it contradicts reality, it does not depart from reality;
because it contradicts reality, it is not a functional activity.
This is the sixth [point].
The explanation of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) and original non-enlightenment (*aprakṛti-āśraya*) each has three sections.
First, the opening of their meanings.
Second, by way of arising;
third, by way of conjunction.
Regarding the first:
Fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) has three meanings:
first, the meaning of being without non-enlightenment;
second, the meaning of possessing fundamental enlightenment.
Third is the meaning of original enlightenment without basis.
Non-enlightenment also has three meanings.
First is the meaning of original enlightenment without basis.
Second is the meaning of non-awakening;
third is the meaning of extinguishing non-awakening.
Regarding "the second is due to arising":
Because there is no non-enlightenment,
there exists original enlightenment; because original enlightenment exists, [there is non-enlightenment].
Because it is established as non-awakening due to the establishment of non-awakening,
it is called "fundamental non-awakening" (mūla-anabodhi). Because of this fundamental non-awakening, [it is so named].
There can be non-awakening;
because of the existence of non-awakening,
there can be the cessation of nature.
Therefore, it is called the cessation of non-awakening.
Furthermore, because within non-awakening there exists the principle of fundamental awakening,
the principle of fundamental awakening can be attained.
Furthermore, because within original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) there is the principle that non-enlightenment (an-awakening) does not exist,
it is possible for non-enlightenment to be extinguished.
Moreover, because within original enlightenment there is the principle of original enlightenment itself, [it is established].
Within non-awakening, there exists the principle of original awakening as both being and non-being.
Furthermore, the various meanings mentioned above are mutually dependent; each is non-dual.
Together they form three propositions.
Furthermore, based on fundamental awakening, non-awakening is established;
this non-awakening is able to cognize names and meanings.
One attains initial enlightenment (*ādikṣayabodhi*).
Because initial enlightenment is accomplished,
non-enlightenment (*abodhi*) is extinguished.
Because non-enlightenment is extinguished through initial enlightenment,
and because initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment, there is no initial enlightenment once one is identical to original enlightenment.
Because there is no initial awakening,
there is no non-awakening.
Because there is no non-awakening...
Then there is no gate of birth and extinction;
there is only the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, one should know that when reaching the source of the mind, [only this remains].
It is solely true thusness (tathatā).
It is without arising or ceasing;
because it is without arising or ceasing.
Nor can True Suchness (tathatā) be said to have distinctions among the three bodies (trikāya).
It is merely in accordance with the defiled capacities of sentient beings that such distinctions appear.
Therefore, it is said that the three bodies are equal.
Regarding the seventh section on the arising of the two marks through following defilement,
the question is asked:
Question: By what defilement does this characteristic arise?
Answer: There are three such [defilements].
First, the characteristic of the purity of wisdom:
following the power of the perfuming of ignorance within one's own mind,
it gives rise to inconceivable karma.
Manifesting forms and transformative functions in accordance with the capacities of those subject to defilement;
second, both of these arise in accordance with one's own defilements,
and by severing one's own defilements [they are transcended].
Only then can its function arise;
the same applies to the inconceivable aspect of its activity.
Within its own defilement, it follows accordingly.
Third, all are concomitant with the defilement of others;
that is to say, when Bodhisattvas cultivate the ten thousand practices to attain the fruit of Buddhahood and so forth, all such matters exist because they follow the ignorance of sentient beings.
If one were to set aside the capacity for defilement...
This is precisely the mark of a single flavor, wherein there is neither cultivation nor attainment.
The eighth question:
Since original enlightenment is suchness, [how is it that...]
Why is it called "awakening" (bodhi)?
Answer: Generally speaking, the term "awakening" has two meanings.
First is the meaning of awakening,
which means that one cannot be defiled by afflictions;
this is precisely the meaning of severing hindrances.
Second is the meaning of awakening-illumination,
which refers to the self-substance manifesting and illuminating all phenomena;
it is the meaning of discerning penetration.
However, as for defilement, it is primordially free from it;
as for virtue, it has never manifested separately.
Therefore, its meaning is inherently possessed from the very beginning.
Therefore, it is called "original enlightenment" (mūla-awakening).
Furthermore, by virtue of these two meanings,
one eliminates the two obstacles.
This reveals two fruits,
both of which are accomplished by nature.
Within initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*), there are likewise two meanings identical to those previously mentioned.
The only difference is the arising of initial awakening (ādi-bodhi);
once defilement is exhausted, initial awakening is not different from original awakening (mūla-bodhi).
Why is this? It is because of two reasons.
First, because this non-existence arises from fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi).
Because it is formed according to defilement and lacks a separate nature,
the two types of awakening reach the source of the mind.
Because it is identical to original enlightenment (mūla-abhisambodhi), there is no distinction from initial enlightenment (ādi-abhisambodhi).
Therefore, there is only one enlightenment that possesses these two meanings.
Furthermore, when this meaning is investigated to its conclusion,
it likewise lacks two characteristics;
namely, the manifestation of defilement and the separation from qualities.
Since defilement is immediately transcended upon its manifestation,
there is only the single true awakening.
Furthermore, because the nature of defilement is inherently transcendent.
There is no defilement to be abandoned;
the nature of virtue is naturally manifest.
There is no virtue to be displayed.
Therefore, its true awakening is without the act of awakening.
For this reason, it is far removed from both the subject that awakens and the object awakened;
yet, though without awakening, it is not unmanifest.
One is called a Buddha because of awakening to all things.
The ninth gate, the True Suchness (Tathatā), is explained according to its fundamental meaning. Thus the text says:
All sentient beings are fundamentally and eternally abiding in entry into nirvana;
there is no meaning of "initial awakening.
This [distinction] is spoken of solely in terms of that which is produced through cultivation.
Because that which was originally non-existent now exists is termed "initial awakening" (shijue).
As for the meaning of "original awakening" (benjue),
it is explained in terms of that which is originally present through cultivation and arising.
Because original enlightenment (hon-gaku) is taught in contrast to initial enlightenment (shiki),

one should understand from the text that the "purity of wisdom" and other such characteristics are explained in terms of that which is originally present versus that which is produced through cultivation.
Therefore, the text says:
"Because fundamental awakening, following along with defilement, gives rise to two aspects.
Question:
Question: What is the difference between the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) and initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*)? Answer:
In reality, they are not distinct.
Because initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) is precisely the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) functioning in accordance with defilement,
it is said that there is a difference based on the distinct nature of their respective objects of reference.
Regarding "differentiation" (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to how original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), in relation to defilement, constitutes the purity of wisdom;
by counteracting defilement, it returns to its original state.
It is the counterpart to the original awakening (mūla-avabodha),
and is termed initial awakening (ādi-avabodha);
furthermore, it is through original awakening that initial awakening is established.
There is no other dharma apart from this; for this reason,
it is collectively termed "primordial existence" (hon-yū).
Regardless of the gate of True Suchness (tathatā),
this refers merely to the "original" [nature] as spoken of within the context of the arising and ceasing of dependent origination;
furthermore, it is because initial awakening (ādikṣaya-bodhi) accords with the original.
Only then is it called original enlightenment;
if it were separated from initial enlightenment,
nothing at all would be established.
Based on this meaning, it is collectively termed "produced through cultivation.
Furthermore, it is originally designated as "initial awakening" (ādi-bodhi).
To speak of the original name as "cultivation" and the fundamental as "innate" is synonymous with this:
it is solely dependent origination.
It is like a perfect sphere;
whichever door one opens,
there is nothing that is not encompassed within it.
The tenth causal condition has three meanings:
first, purity of mind is the cause,
and ignorance is the condition.
Second, false objects serve as conditions,
and the fundamental consciousness serves as the cause;
these two are as explained in the commentary.
The three [aspects] take prior causes and conditions as their cause and subsequent causes and conditions as their condition,
because they have been fundamentally integrated within the one mind.
Reflect upon this accordingly.
In this context, "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya) carries only the sense of that from which something arises.
It is not distinct from the arising and ceasing of that which is produced;
when that mind is conjoined with ignorance,
it constitutes the causal condition.
Nor is there any separate dharma;
it is simply by gathering and accumulating these various dharmas that what is called a "sentient being" is formed.
This means that true mind constitutes the substance of sentient beings,
while the five mental faculties and consciousness constitute their characteristics;
therefore, there is only the one mind.
"Mind" has the sense of being a basis.
The first three are the bases of both the fundamental and the derivative;
that is to say, the derivative depends upon the fundamental.
The first is named "mind" (manas);
the latter two are the bases for the coarse and the subtle,
because the coarse depends upon the subtle.
That which is subtle is called "mind" (manas);
coarse consciousness has no further basis upon which it depends,
and therefore it is not called "mind."
It is merely the act of discernment;
it is simply called "consciousness.
As for the phrase "the three realms are mind-only":
This refers to the integration of the root and its branches;
it means that the five mental states of the pure mind,
as well as consciousness and so forth, all arise from the mind.
That which arises from a non-associated mind is called the arising of false thought;
that which arises from an associated mind is [the arising of true thought].
Because the corresponding mind takes as its object the realm of the *ālayavijñāna* (the manifest consciousness) among the three subtle [consciousnesses],
there is no external object outside the mind that can be discriminated;
therefore, it is said that one discriminates one's own mind.
When one realizes that the object of perception is nothing but mind,
the mind ultimately does not grasp itself;
thus, the mind as a subject of cognition is exhausted.
Therefore it is said that "the mind does not see the mind.
When ignorance gives rise to objects of cognition,
this is the time when the true mind is conjoined with ignorance.
Because they are able to grasp their own intrinsically pure nature,
only a Buddha thoroughly understands it;
those on the stages (bhūmi) realize one portion of it through direct realization.
Therefore, it is said that they know only a small portion.
Gross afflictions arise based on subtle afflictions;
subtle afflictions, however, have no further basis upon which they depend.
Therefore, it is said that they "suddenly arise.
This is because, within the same scripture, it is stated that there is no beginning to ignorance (*avidyā*);
since no defiled phenomena have a beginning other than ignorance, [they are said to arise suddenly].
Question:
Since ignorance moves true suchness to form the defiled mind,
why is it that the defiled mind takes ignorance as its condition?
Distinguishing coarse and subtle according to their stages,
the true mind is their cause; therein,
no distinction of superiority or inferiority is made.
Answer: Because defiled phenomena possess distinctions,
whereas the true mind is of a single flavor.
Fundamental wisdom is of two types:
first, the wisdom of conforming to suchness that arises through cultivation;
second, the wisdom of the original enlightenment of suchness itself.
Worldly knowledge is also twofold:
first, the knowledge of things as they are (yathāvadbhāva-jñāna) produced through cultivation;
second, the knowledge that follows defilement (anuvartana-jñāna).
Because the defiled mind is agitated and thus violates the wisdom of the non-moving, equal, and fundamental awakening,
it is called the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, because ignorance does not realize that movement is itself stillness,
one is unable to discern within movement; this is the obstruction of wisdom.
In the eleventh [section], regarding the characteristic of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), ignorance has two meanings.
First, it is universal;
second, it can bring about the two minds.
Second, the distinction:
because it can bring about the subtle mind,
it is said that "because ignorance ceases, the objective realm ceases."
It is further stated that because ignorance ceases, the non-associated mind ceases.
The object of perception (*ālambana*) also has two meanings:
first, it is universal.
This is what is accomplished.
There are two distinctions:
they can give rise to three types of coarse minds.
Therefore, ignorance has both a general capacity and a specific capacity;
its object has both a general scope and a specific scope.
Consequently, the object is both the agent and the recipient.
Ignorance is merely the absence of what is not there.
This is the twelfth [point].
Among the four types of perfuming:
The perfuming of defilement is also twofold:
the first is general,
and the latter is specific.
Regarding the statement that "prior to and within [the state of] ignorance, the true nature is permeated by delusion,
giving rise to the false mind," this refers to the *karmic mark* (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). "The arising of non-awakened thought" refers to...
The ability to perceive is the characteristic of seeing.
That which manifests as delusory objects is the characteristic of the objective realm.
This belongs to the three subtle states.
What is now termed "thought" (念) refers to the first two of the six coarse states.
The author’s [position] is the second of the two [subsequent views].
The latter two are as stated in the treatise. Regarding the specific [distinctions]:
"Those that increase mindfulness" refers to the first two among the six coarse [factors].
"Grasping" refers to...
The next two are [the second and third].
The final two are the fruits of karma;
they are not the subject under discussion here.
If that is so, why did the preceding passage state that the six aspects arise because of objective conditions?
The explanation says:
The previous passage was based on a general discussion;
this one concerns specific distinctions,
as it treats the latter two as the transformative functions of the deluded mind.
It does not arise from objects independent of conditions.
Within the perfuming of the deluded mind,
the karmic consciousness (karmavijñāna) encompasses all three subtle states.
Regarding "that which is named from the beginning as perfuming":
it perfumes fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā),
because its deluded movement is subtle.
Because one undergoes the suffering of the karma of transformation based on this subtle movement of karma,
the Sūtra says:
This refers to the fact that, with the ground of the abiding of ignorance as the condition and outflow-free karma as the cause,
one obtains the retribution of the transformation body (*pariṇāmi-kāya*). This is what is meant.
Within the *karmic consciousness* (*kṛtya-vijñāna*), there are likewise three types of coarseness:
the ignorance that perfumes the branches and tips [of existence],
the coarse movement of creating karma, and [the resulting state].
This refers to the suffering of fragmented existence.
Fundamental ignorance deludes the rational nature and perfumes the *tathatā*.
The three factors, beginning with the formation of karma,
are the branches; ignorance, deluded regarding objects,

Answer: This should be treated as four propositions.
First, that which is exclusively pure.

Second, those that are invariably defiled,
because sentient beings who follow the stream have not yet awakened their ignorance.
Third, neither defiled nor pure;
this refers to the ineffable *tathatā*.
Fourth, both defiled and pure.
This is because both its characteristics and its functions are vast;
furthermore, it is defiled,
manifesting as an illusory appearance that follows the conditions of the preceding stages and the capacities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, because it is pure,
and because True Suchness remains unchanging in accordance with conditions,
regarding these four propositions:
It is not the fourth alternative;
it is the third alternative.
It is not the third alternative.
This constitutes the fourth alternative;

Chapter Four: The Four Denials. These four denials arise because ordinary beings are deluded regarding causes and conditions.
The first is the denial by way of superimposition (*samāropa*).
Second is the slander of impairment;
third is the slander of contradiction;
fourth is the slander of frivolous discourse; and [fifth] is the slander of superimposition.
Now, when one examines all phenomena,
they arise from causes and conditions;
because there is no creator.
At the time of its arising, it does not abide,
because it lacks intrinsic nature; thus,
it is beyond the reach of conceptual construction.
The nature of all phenomena is thus;
it cannot be grasped or clung to.
Yet, ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles—
When all phenomena arise,
one grasps them as existing; however,
they are merely phenomena produced by causes and conditions.
Its nature is free from existence;
it is apart from the phenomena of existence.
To grasp at and declare that it exists—this is [the error].
Because it does not accord with reason,
it is called the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*). Since this constitutes slander, [it is so designated].
This is not reasonable; the meaning is likewise incorrect.
Such is the nature of causes and conditions.
Although its nature exists,
when conditions arise and manifest before one,
it cannot be said to be non-existent.
To insist that something is non-existent with respect to a phenomenon that is not non-existent is irrational.
To claim [either] existence or non-existence is to commit the fault of slander; since both existence and non-existence are errors,
it must be the principle that [reality] is both existent and non-existent.
He replied:
"Causes and conditions are a single dharma;
their nature is not mutually contradictory."
That which is non-contradictory is called the principle of dependent origination;
it is a phenomenon whose nature is characterized by both existence and non-existence.
This is not a causal condition.
Because it is not a causal condition,
it constitutes a contradiction and a denial.
To hold that something both exists and does not exist is contrary to the Dharma and does not accord with the vision of reality.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent should accord with principle.
He replied: "In discussing the principles of reality,
they are manifested by means of causes and conditions."
To say it is neither existent nor non-existent is outside the realm of causes and conditions;
such a position is not logical.
To toy with all phenomena is called the slander of frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*). For,
indeed, conceptualization involves making distinctions.
That which accords with grasping and rejecting is entirely a mental construction;
it does not correspond to the true principle.
To be free from mental activity and to sever all signs is called the Middle Way.
Therefore, a sutra says:

The dharma of causes and conditions is free from both existence and non-existence. *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra-piṇḍārtha* (A Separate Record of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna).
